The overnight bus from Jaipur to Delhi had no working lights and no charging point, and Suraj's phone was at thirty percent. He had meant to sleep. Instead he opened the news and found the landslide story: a school bus buried, parents digging with bare hands, a boy's shoe in the mud.
The signal kept dropping, so each video loaded in pieces, and he kept waiting, refreshing, waiting. He read every update until the battery died at two in the morning. Then he sat in the dark with his forehead on the cold window.
At the Delhi stop his friend Wasim, sleepy in the next seat, stretched. "You look like you haven't slept."
"I haven't."
"Exams?"
Suraj shook his head. He felt heavy all the way down to his feet and couldn't say why. He didn't know those people. There was nothing he could have done from a bus.

Counselling centre note, Friday.
Gopika, nineteen, second year, came in today with her friend Vaibhav, who waited outside. She said she has felt "heavy and on edge" since Sunday but "nothing is wrong". Sleeping late. Snapping at her roommate.
When I asked what she'd been doing in the evenings, she said she'd been following the earthquake news. Videos, rescue clips, families searching. Three or four hours a night. She had no family there and knew no one affected.
She said, "I feel stupid. It's not even my pain."
I told her that feeling others' pain is a sign of care, not stupidity, and that it can soak in when we can't do anything.
What I did next: we made a small plan — news once a day, not at night, and she chose one relief fund her college was collecting for. She'll come back Tuesday.

qa.a: She felt foolish and confused, weighed down by strangers' suffering she couldn't explain.

A fire in a city factory. A child missing in another state. A clip of people crying outside a hospital. None of them were people he knew.

Tenzin nodded. "The phone brings everybody's worst day to you. And you can't do anything with it."
